But before we do that, so we've talked about kind of these early days of hiring your first two reps, getting your VP of sales to help scale out the team. To give people a sense of where this goes, as the business scales, what does the org evolution look like? You have these two reps doing sales on their own, then you have a manager. What does it look like over the next couple phases of the sales org?
turns.zh: 我能想象这代表什么意思。哦，挺有意思的。之前没听过这个术语。好，我先退一步，转到另一个话题。但在结束之前，我们聊了聊招聘前两位销售代表、让VP of Sales帮忙扩展团队的初期阶段。为了让大家更清楚后续的发展路径，随着业务规模扩大，组织架构会如何演变？先是两位销售代表独立开展销售，然后引入经理。接下来几个阶段的销售组织会是什么样子？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Look, to simplify, there's rules of eight. So in sales, I'm actually not sure what the tip of heuristic is in product, because product teams are leaner, at least I hope. I like it when they're leaner. But the thing about sales is there's no efficiency. If you have a sales-led motion, half your company is going to be in sales at 10 millionaire, half your company is going to be in sales at 50, half your company is going to be in sales at 100. (01:00:27): One of the tough parts of the software model is that there's no, there's actually almost anti-efficiencies in sales. The public companies are actually less, they have the higher CACs than startups, believe it or not, because they have so much market penetration. So you're going to need a lot of people. And it's rules of eight, eight SDRs, outbound reps need one manager, eight AEs, eight sales execs need a director above them. (01:00:51): And then when you really scale, eight directors. You don't really ever going to have eight directors, but eight directors could have a VP or eight reports. And so there's rules of eight. If you want to build an organization on it, it's all rules of eight. For a while, for SDRs, thinking this was this high velocity entry-level position, people pushed it to 12. But the more folks I talk to today, the more I hear, everyone's reverted to eight. I'd rather have fewer SDRs, having better conversations. And so it's just, you can build your whole org with eights.
turns.zh: 听着，说得简单点，有个“八人法则”。在销售领域，我其实不太清楚产品团队的启发式思维是什么，因为产品团队通常规模更小，至少我希望如此。我更倾向于团队规模更精简。但销售部门效率低下。如果你推行以销售为主导的策略，当公司规模达到1000万美元时，半数员工会从事销售；当规模达到5000万美元时，半数员工还是销售；当达到1亿美元时，同样比例的员工继续从事销售。（01:00:27）软件行业的难点之一是，销售环节几乎存在反效率效应。上市公司实际上效率更低，其客户获取成本比初创公司更高——信不信由你，因为它们的市场渗透度更高。所以你需要大量人手。按照“八人法则”，八个销售开发代表需要一个经理，八个外呼代表需要一个主管，八个客户经理需要一个总监。（01:00:51）当规模进一步扩大时，八个总监可能会上报给一位副总裁或八位下属。整个组织结构都是基于“八人法则”构建的。曾有人试图将SDR职位设为高速度入门级职位，但后来发现更多人回归到八人法则。我宁愿减少SDR数量，提升对话质量。整个组织可以完全围绕“八人法则”来构建。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is way too easy of an answer. So the idea there is you hire this VP of sales, then you hire six more sales reps, AEs. So what happens next? You hire another-
turns.zh: 这答案也太简单了。所以思路是先聘请销售副总裁，然后再招六个销售代表、客户经理。接下来呢？再招一个经理。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Got to start hiring managers.
turns.zh: 对，得开始招经理了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Manager, got it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 明白了。是的。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then you scale eight more reps.
turns.zh: 然后再扩展八个销售代表。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: And once you have eight AEs scaled, you almost always are going to start, a VP's going to already... A good VP of sales already be hunting two directors.
turns.zh: 当八个客户经理扩展到位后，VP通常已经在招两位总监了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two directors.
turns.zh: 两位总监。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Whether they're just split up normally, whether they're east, west is a classic way. Another way, you might have smaller and larger customers. That's pretty standard, right? Commercial and enterprise. But a good VP of sales, once you have, she or he has eight reports, will be bringing in two directors, or maybe two VPs if they're an SVP. There's a lot of title-
turns.zh: 无论是正常分工，还是按区域划分，都是经典模式。另一种方式是根据客户规模进行分级。商业客户和企业客户的区分很常见，对吧？但优秀的销售副总裁一旦手下有八个下属，就会引入两位总监，如果是SVP，可能还会有两位VP。职级层级很多——

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: ... directors or maybe two VPs if they're an SVP. There's a lot of title inflation today, which doesn't bother me nearly as much as a lot of other things we've chatted about. I don't care what your title is if you'll actually do sales or do work, but yeah, we need to bring in managers at 8:00. And folks that can, also, a related point is, a lot of founders were, "When will my ... " I really love my head of sales, but she's a stretch. Most of them should be stretches. (01:02:25): If you hire the seasoned one, they're not going to work, so for 95 out of 100 of us, our first head of sales should be a stretch VP of Sales. And what that means is, usually, they were a director before that or a senior director or sort of a VP, okay? But you should be cautious about hiring your first VP of Sales for their first third VP of Sales gig. They're not willing to do the job anymore. You need a stretch and it's worth it for their career growth. It's worth it for their personal growth. It's worth it for the equity, right? So you're going to hire a stretch. That's an important tip right there. But then, you're going to be a little worried, how far can Lenny go? How far can ... I love Lenny, but he was a director for two years before this, and this is his first rule, and he did so good last year, but I'm worried Lenny's going to break. I'm worried Lenny's going to break. (01:03:09): And related to this quote, the simple answer is, Lenny will break if he can't source those directors under him. You can scale forever as a sales leader if you can hire better managers under you. And it's true of any functional area, but what you'll see in sales is, you'll see your stretch VP of Sales drown when they never can hire better managers under them, They'll end up doing some weird internal promotions, which you want, you want to do internal promotions. My rule is you want to promote 50% from within and hire 50% without for your managers, but if, really, the only people you can promote are just junior people on your team, you can't find leaders, you can't scale. I do see this happen too frequently is, a first time out of sales, does it, and then, they're like, "Here are my managers, Lorraine and Jason, but they really were just reps for two years and they don't know how to do it." So you have a whole bunch of people who don't know how to do it. That's when the organization cracks.
turns.zh: ……如果是SVP，可能就需要两位VP了。如今职位头衔虚高成风，这倒不像其他我们讨论过的问题那样让我感到困扰。只要你能实际参与销售或做实事，我不在乎你的头衔是什么。不过是的，我们8点就得把经理们召集起来。还有一点值得注意的是，很多创始人曾问：“我的……何时能到位？”我很欣赏我的销售主管，但她确实是个挑战。大多数人本就该面临挑战。（01:02:25）：如果你聘用经验丰富的老手，他们未必愿意投入工作。所以对我们中95%的人来说，首位销售主管应该是个挑战性的VP级别。这意味着，他们此前通常是总监、资深总监或VP级别。但你得谨慎考虑首位VP的任命——这往往是他们首次担任VP级别职位的机会。他们可能已心灰意冷，渴望突破自我。这对他们的职业发展、个人成长乃至股权激励都意义重大。所以你会选择挑战性人才。这是关键建议。但随之而来的是担忧：莱尼能走多远？我很喜欢莱尼，但他此前只担任了两年总监，而这是他首个VP级别职位。他去年表现出色，但我担心他会力不从心。（01:03:09）：回到这个话题，简单答案是：如果莱尼无法培养出下属总监，他必将崩盘。若能招到优秀的下属管理者，销售团队就能持续扩张。这适用于任何职能部门，但在销售领域，挑战性VP若无法培养优秀下属，最终只能通过内部晋升来维持现状。这是不可取的。我的规则是，管理层50%从内部晋升，50%外部招聘。但如果团队里只有初级人员可晋升，组织就无法扩张。我见过太多新手销售创始人一开始就搞砸了，然后说：“这是我的下属洛林和杰森，但他们不过是做了两年的销售代表，根本不懂得管理。”最终导致整个团队无所适从。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Imagine a place where you can find all your potential customers and get your message in front of them in a cost efficient way. If you're a B2B business, that place exists, and it's called LinkedIn. LinkedIn ads allows you to build the right relationships, drive results and reach your customers in a respectful environment. Two of my portfolio companies, Webflow and Census, are LinkedIn success stories. Census had a 10x increase in pipeline with a LinkedIn startup team. For Webflow, after ramping up on LinkedIn in Q4, they had the highest marketing source revenue quarter to date. With LinkedIn ads, you'll have direct access to and can build relationships with decision makers, including 950 million members, 180 million senior execs, and over 10 million C-level executives. You'll be able to drive results with targeting and measurement tools built specifically for B2B. In tech, LinkedIn generated 2x to 5x higher return on ad spend than any other social media platforms. Audiences on LinkedIn have two times the buying power of the average web audience, and you'll work with a partner who respects the B2B world you operate in. (01:05:11): Make B2B marketing everything it can be and get $100 credit on your next campaign. Just go to linkedin.com/podlenny to claim your credit. That's linkedin.com/podlenny. Terms and conditions apply. (01:05:26): There's these terms that we throw, around account executive reps. It might be helpful just to give people a sense of what does this actually mean when someone's an account executive. Is it that they're just sitting there calling and doing sales directly? Whatever the key terms are for the roles or the title might be helpful to quickly summarize.
turns.zh:
想象一个能让您精准锁定潜在客户，并以高性价比方式将信息传递给他们的平台。如果您是B2B企业，这个平台就叫做LinkedIn。LinkedIn广告能助您建立正确的客户关系、推动业务成果，并在尊重的商业环境中触达目标客户。我的两家投资组合公司——Webflow和Census——就是LinkedIn营销的成功典范。Census通过组建专门的LinkedIn团队，销售线索量激增了10倍；而Webflow在第四季度加大LinkedIn投放力度后，创下了迄今为止最高的营销渠道收入纪录。通过LinkedIn广告，您将直接接触并建立与决策者的联系——平台拥有9.5亿用户，其中1.8亿是高管用户，1000多万是C级高管。借助专为B2B场景打造的定向投放和效果监测工具，您能高效达成营销目标。在科技领域，LinkedIn广告的广告支出回报率比其他社交媒体平台高出2至5倍。LinkedIn平台用户的购买力是普通网民的两倍，您还将与深谙B2B商业逻辑的合作伙伴携手共进。（01:05:11）：助力B2B营销释放全部潜力，下次广告投放即可获得100美元优惠。立即访问linkedin.com/podlenny即可领取优惠。条款与条件适用。
（01:05:26）：我们常提及的职位名称，如“客户经理”和“销售代表”，可能让新人难以理解。能否简要解释这些职位的含义？比如，客户经理是否就是负责打电话直接销售的？对于这些职位或头衔的关键术语做个快速总结或许会有帮助。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Yeah, I think the two ones that are probably less obvious for folks that are new are SDR, Sales development representative, and AE, account executive.
turns.zh: 是的，对于新手来说，可能不太熟悉的两个职位是SDR（销售开发代表）和AE（客户经理）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great.
turns.zh: 好的，明白了。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: And SDR is, generally, although I wish it wasn't, it is generally an entry level position, often fresh out of school, generally paid on the order of 60K to 80K, OTE and SaaS and US-based SaaS, and their job is to email for dollars, dial for dollars, and in many cases, to screen, to screen inbound leads. It's entry level, and their job is to pass on a lead to a sales executive, an account executive, an AE. Not all companies have SDRs. It's a longer topic, but pretty much all the best teams have some type of SDR function now because we've learned we want to specialize. We want openers opening and we want closers closing, so that's the rough idea. (01:06:34): SDRs are openers in some cases, and account executives are the more seasoned folks closing. And it varies, compensation from account executives that are US-based could be anywhere from like 90K to 200K, depending on, that's with base and bonus split at 50/50, depending on whether they're hunting tiny deals or big ones. That's the way an account executive works. And I think what doesn't happen today ... Those are the acronyms, SDR and AE. I think people can figure out VP of Sales, that's vice president of sales. (01:07:03): I think a thing that's gone on in the industry that founders expect now because there's so much discussion of it on LinkedIn and social media, but I haven't found work, is that an account executive will magically be full stack. They will do outbound themselves, they'll go use ZoomInfo and Apollo and develop a list themselves, they'll manage that outbound list themselves. If they don't have enough inbound, in their free time, you know what they'll do, Lenny, in their free time? They'll just do more outbound. You know what sales reps do in their free time? Today, they sell real estate or courses. (01:07:36): If you want a tip, for founders, I know you want this full stack AE, and they do exist when they're micromanaged in certain high performance sales organizations, but they don't exist in real life. They're specialized. Most AEs, they want to be closers, they want to be handed a lead, a contact me, a lead. They want to work the lead and close the lead, and you hire some SDRs to help generate more demand. Those are the basic acronyms. What's hard for most founders, here's the tough part, most founders have enough stamina to manage a couple of these AEs, these account executives, these folks who work the leads. Most founders do not have the stamina to manage 10 kids fresh out of college that need to be micromanaged on an hourly basis to call leads. Very, very few founders themselves can manage a team of SDRs, but if you can, it's like a superpower.
turns.zh:
销售开发代表（SDR）通常被视为入门级职位——尽管我希望并非如此，但这种情况确实普遍存在。新入职的应届生往往会担任这一职位，年薪通常在6万至8万美元之间。SDR的主要职责包括通过邮件获取潜在客户、进行电话营销，以及筛选潜在客户。他们的核心任务是将潜在客户转交给销售主管、客户经理或高级销售代表（AE）处理。并非所有公司都设有SDR部门。这是个复杂的话题，但如今大多数优秀团队都建立了某种形式的SDR职能，因为我们意识到需要专业化分工。销售团队需要专人负责开拓客户（Openers）和完成交易（Closers），这就是基本思路。

（01:06:34）：在某些情况下，SDR负责开拓客户，而客户经理则负责更成熟的交易跟进。薪资方面，美国客户经理的收入范围通常在9万至20万美元之间，底薪与奖金比例为50/50，具体取决于他们追逐的是小型交易还是大型项目。这就是客户经理的日常工作。

（01:07:03）：当前行业存在一个误区，创始人们期望销售团队成员能具备全能技能——比如自主开展外拓营销、自主开发客户名单、自主管理名单库。但现实并非如此。创始人们往往期望客户经理能无所不能，却忽视了现实：如果客户经理手头潜在客户不足，他们就会在空闲时间继续开展外拓营销。如今，销售代表们要么转行卖房、卖课程，要么干脆离职。

（01:07:36）：给创始们一个建议：你们想招全能型客户经理？这种情况在高效销售组织中确实存在，但现实中少之又少。销售团队需要专业化分工。大多数客户经理只想专注于交易闭合，不想处理潜在客户开发。SDR的职责就是协助生成更多潜在客户。这些是基本术语。最难的部分在于，大多数创始人有足够耐心管理几个客户经理，但很少有人能同时管理10个刚毕业、需要每小时微管理的外拓团队。能做到这一点的人，堪称超人般的存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was really helpful. I did not know what exactly these terms represented, and when you're hiring those first two reps, they should be at the account executive level.
turns.zh: 这真的很有帮助。我之前不知道这些术语具体代表什么意思，当你招聘前两位销售代表时，他们应该达到客户经理级别。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Yes. And they'll do some outbound and they'll do some of this SDR work. It's just, ultimately, people end up specializing.
turns.zh: 是的。他们会做一些外拓工作，也会承担部分SDR的职责。但最终，人们还是会走向专业化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the title for someone above the account executive? Is it Director of Sales?
turns.zh: 客户经理之上的职位叫什么？是销售总监吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Yeah. There's really no ... It's a meta topic. I wish there were another career path for these ICs. This does exist in product, it does exist in engineering. It should exist in sales, but the truth is it doesn't. There is no senior SDR for this outbound. And for this AE, this person closing, yes, you can go more enterprise and make more money, but there isn't really a senior AE track, but there should be. It's unfortunate. It should be. (01:09:15): Too many of these folks are looking for, they look to go into management for promotion when what they really should look for is to be a super IC, and it's a shame that more folks don't try to implement a super IC role in sales, but that's basically what the career path is in management. And that's why another tip, another mistake that founders often make is, they hire the number one account executive at a hot company to be their head of sales. It's not the same skills. Most sales executives should not be managers. They don't want to be managers. They want to be individuals. They want to be highly paid individual contributors, these days, that mostly work from home and make a lot of money working 30 hours a week. That does not naturally breed great management skills.
turns.zh: 是啊。这真的没有……这是一个元话题。我真希望这些IC（内部客户）能有另一种职业发展路径。在产品部门有，在工程部门有，在销售部门也应该有，但现实并非如此。这种外向型销售模式没有高级SDR（销售开发代表）职位。而对于AE（客户成功经理）来说，虽然可以转型做更偏向企业客户的销售赚更多钱，但实际上并没有高级AE的晋升通道，本该有的。这太遗憾了。（01:09:15）：太多人一心想晋升管理层，却忽视了他们真正该追求的是成为超级IC。令人惋惜的是，更多人没有尝试在销售部门设立超级IC角色，而这恰恰是管理层的晋升路径。因此，创始人常犯的另一个错误是：从热门公司挖来头号AE担任销售负责人。但这两者的技能要求截然不同。大多数销售高管不应成为管理者。他们不想当管理者，他们想成为高收入的个体贡献者，如今这类人大多在家办公，每周工作30小时就能赚大钱。这种模式并不能自然培养出优秀的管理技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to shift directions a little bit and talk about product and sales. A lot of listeners of this podcast are product managers or founders building products. How involved should product managers be in sales. And vice versa, how involved should sales be in the roadmap and what's being built?
turns.zh: 接下来我想转换一下话题，谈谈产品和销售。这档播客的许多听众都是产品经理或创业者，他们在打造产品。产品经理应该在多大程度上参与销售？反之，销售又应该在多大程度上参与路线图规划和产品开发？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: I think, in the best run B2B organizations that I've worked with, and my own as well, the great, at least the head of product, the VP of Products, are deeply involved in sales. Deeply involved in sales. Deeply involved in sales. A company I invested in that's just crossing $60 million, they just had a meeting with who will be their largest customer. And the head of product who was there at the board meeting is like, "Thank God I was there because what they want to do with our product, we sort of do. We sort of." Now, the product does do it, but what they want to basically do is deconstruct the product. They don't actually want to use the backend and analytics and some other pieces, but they don't really need the front end of the product. If the head of product hadn't been there, that deal would've been lost. It would've been lost. (01:11:11): An AE doesn't know that. Even if an AE did know that, a sales rep did know that even. If the VP of Sales didn't know ... A VP of Sales would not be empowered enough to stand up in a meeting and say, "I know what you want. We can launch tomorrow on this and, in 90 days, we'll tweak the UI so it does exactly what you want." You want that in your big deals. If you have that magical VP of Product that truly owns the roadmap, owns it and has the gravitas for that meeting, they become like the mini CEO in these meetings. A lot of CEOs, at scale, I've talked to, I was just talking with Daniel Chait at Greenhouse, he does this, they're over $200 million, when they have that head of product, they divide and conquer with the big customers. And the CEO can do some and the VP of product can do others. (01:11:52): And sometimes, the VP of Eng, if they're very producty, can also do that role too. Sometimes, you get these three weapons. In the old days, sometimes, your VP of Customer Success could do this, but unfortunately, and I know this is going to trigger some people, I don't see customer success stepping up for this pseudo product role anymore and I see them shrinking more and more into process. But that magical VP product, they give you that scale, that CEO level scale. (01:12:17): Can a product manager or a director do that? In my experience, the best ones, absolutely. The mid-pack ones that are working on the color of the pixel, I'd rather not have them in the deal. You have to be utterly fluent in the product, the entire product. You have to be the one that knows how to connect the pieces that don't ought to always connect themselves, and you have to have the gravitas to work with a large customer, to make commitments. That deep knowledge and commitment, it's hard below the VP level, but if it does exist, I love it. They become one of the greatest strategic weapons of a B2B company is bringing the product team, because the VP of Sales never quite goes that deep and can't make the commits, and the CEO can't be everywhere.
turns.zh: 我认为，在我合作过的优秀B2B公司（包括我自己所在的公司），至少产品负责人、产品副总裁会深度参与销售工作。深度参与销售工作。深度参与销售工作。一家我投资的公司刚突破6000万美元营收，他们刚和最大的客户开会。出席董事会会议的产品负责人说：“谢天谢地我当时在场，因为他们想用我们的产品做的事，我们其实已经能做到了。我们能做到。”虽然产品确实能实现部分功能，但他们想做的其实是解构产品。他们并不需要后端分析等模块，但前端界面对他们来说就足够了。如果产品负责人当时不在场，那笔交易可能就黄了。黄了。（01:11:11）：销售代表不知道这些。即使销售代表知道，销售代表也不知道。销售副总裁如果不了解……销售副总裁没有足够权威在会议上站出来说：“我知道你们的需求。我们明天就能上线，在90天内调整UI，让它完全符合你们的要求。”这正是大单所需要的。如果有那种能真正掌控路线图、具备会议气场的神奇产品副总裁，他们在这些会议中就成了迷你CEO。很多大公司的高管，我刚和Greenhouse的丹尼尔·查特聊过，他们就是这样做的。当有产品负责人在场时，他们就能分工合作拿下大客户。CEO负责一些工作，产品副总裁负责其他部分。（01:11:52）：有时候，如果工程副总裁也具备很强的产品思维，也能胜任这个角色。有时，你能同时拥有这三位高手。在过去，客户成功副总裁有时也能胜任这个角色，但很遗憾——我知道这会激怒一些人——我觉得客户成功部门不再承担这种伪产品角色了，而是越来越专注于流程。但那种神奇的产品副总裁，他们能赋予你CEO级别的影响力。（01:12:17）：产品经理或总监能做到吗？以我的经验，最优秀的肯定能做到。中等水平的那些只管像素颜色的，我宁愿他们别参与交易。你必须对整个产品了如指掌。你必须是那个能把本不该自行衔接的零部件拼合起来的人，还必须有足够的气场与大客户合作、做出承诺。这种深层的知识和承诺，在副总裁级别以下很难达到，但如果真有这样的人，我很欣赏。他们成为B2B公司最强大的战略武器之一，因为销售副总裁永远达不到那种深度，也无法做出承诺，而CEO又无法事事亲力亲为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The bane of many product managers' existence is the flip side of sales is involvement in product. Do you have any advice for how you've seen the best SaaS companies handle requests from sales going into product, how product teams should think about requests from sales and making that work?
turns.zh: 许多产品经理的烦恼之源在于，销售深度参与产品开发的反面是产品深度参与销售工作。对于你见过的优秀SaaS公司如何处理销售提出的产品需求，以及产品团队应如何看待销售的需求并有效应对，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: I think this one is so simple and I'm surprised people make it so complicated. I know we all release 28 times a day, but the reality is, software still goes on quarterly release cycles no matter what we say, okay? Your customers cannot process 88 releases a day, okay? The maximum a customer can process is two big releases a year and maybe quarterly, so let's simplify. That's how customers think. Forget about how we build software. (01:13:46): Every quarter, give your head of sales a certain budget, whether it's story points or 10% of the pie chart, however you do it, give them a budget. And when you do this, things will radically change then. They radically change because even the best VPs of sales, they change the wind. On Monday, what they really need is the HubSpot integration. And they're like, "Oh, my god. We weren't going to do that for two years, but I guess we could change everything on Monday," but then, on Wednesday, a new prospect comes in and, "We need SAP, but we just spent two days spec-ing out." You need SAP. And then, on Monday, it's Salesforce, right? And it's not that sales isn't honest, it's just, the big deals, the big ones always, the tail's wagging the dog and it burns out the organization. Even with the best sales leaders, I find it burns out, especially because the stressful deals, they overreact, and as good as they are, they're not product people, so they don't really know how to prioritize and force rank. If you say, "Okay, Lenny, my VP of Sales, great. HubSpot, SAP, whatever you want, you've got 10% of the budget, you've got a hundred story points, whatever metric or heuristic you use, but you've got to decide now each quarter." And if you want to change during the course of the quarter, if you want to disrupt our whole engineering product team, you can do it, but understand there's a high cost, and the later you do it in the quarter, the less successful it's going to be because we already started the HubSpot integration. Not only will it demoralize the team, but we're going to run out of ... You already used your budget. (01:15:10): I just don't see enough product leaders being objective here, saying, "Listen, here's your budget. You get it, period. No one can take it from you. I guess the CO can steal it if she really wants to, but it's yours, VP of Sales." And they will do the low balancing across their team. They will do it. They will listen and they'll say, "Maybe I don't need that HubSpot integration after all. Maybe." Right? (01:15:32): Because what a VP of Sales should be doing is taking ... The CO has to look five years into the future, product has to look about two years into the future, and you really can't ask a VP of Sales to look more than 12 months into the future because that's where they're next on the line, but a good one will load balance feature requests across the year and they will listen to all the ... Because they'll actually be in sales, they'll actually be in deals, and they'll be listening and they'll realize, look, even though we're going to lose this deal to HubSpot, I've gotten four SAP requests the last ... I'm going to take that bet. Even if I'm wrong, I'm going to take that bet. You got to give them that ... And you got to talk about it every week and say, "Look, here's your budget, Jane. Here's your story points, your whatever, your 10%. This is what we're building now for you, objectively, and this is what we're currently planning for the next two quarters. Would you like to change the ones for the next two quarters? Because we haven't committed any code yet, and if you really want to change what's in process, you can. Otherwise, it's going to be hyper disruptive," but you got to at least pretend to be objective, for sales. (01:16:29): If you're too emotional about it, you break the organization. You've got to say, "Listen, I know we've already written 80% of this upside integration. If you really need us to put us on the shelf and drop everything for a million dollar deal, we're a startup, we'll do it. But understand, just, is this really really what you want?" And if you involve them every week as a stakeholder, magic happens. But I don't see the VPs of Product that I work with, I know I'm not in all the staff meetings, but the meetings I'm in and the board meetings, I don't see this back and forth happening.
turns.zh:
我觉得这事儿太简单了，真搞不懂人们为什么把它搞得这么复杂。我知道我们每天要发布28次，但现实是，无论我们怎么说软件还是按季度发布周期来的，对吧？你的客户不可能一天处理88次发布，最多一年两次大发布，季度一次，所以简单点吧。客户就是这么想的。别管我们怎么开发软件了。（01:13:46）：每个季度给销售主管一个预算，不管是故事点还是占饼图的10%，你想怎么算就怎么算。这样一来，情况会彻底改观。改观是因为即使是最优秀的销售副总裁也会随风而动。周一他们说需要HubSpot集成，周三又有新客户进来要求SAP，而前两天才刚花两天时间做需求分析。SAP才是真正需要的。周一又变成Salesforce了。这不是销售不诚实，而是大单子总是让尾巴摇动狗头，最后把整个组织累垮了。即使是最优秀的销售领导者也会被烧坏，尤其是在高压交易环境下，他们会过度反应。虽说他们很优秀，但毕竟不是产品人，所以他们不擅长优先级排序和强制取舍。如果你说："好的，销售副总裁Lenny，很好。HubSpot、SAP，随你怎么说，你有10%的预算，100个故事点，无论用什么指标或启发式方法，但每个季度你必须现在就决定。"

如果你想在季度中途调整，要想颠覆整个工程团队可以，但要明白成本很高，而且越到季度后期，成功率越低，因为我们已经开始HubSpot集成了。这不仅会打击团队士气，还会导致预算超支。

（01:15:10）：我发现太多产品负责人不够客观，不肯说："听着，预算给你了，就这么定。没人能拿走。总监要是想偷走，也能做到，但这是你的预算，销售副总裁的。"然后他们会在团队内部进行资源平衡。他们会这么做。他们会倾听，然后说："或许HubSpot集成真没必要了。或许吧。"对吧？

（01:15:32）：因为销售副总裁应该做的是统筹……总监要着眼五年，产品要着眼两年，实在不行也别指望销售副总裁能看超过12个月，因为那是他们下一个晋升节点。但优秀的副总裁会全年平衡功能请求，并倾听所有意见。因为他们亲自参与销售，参与交易，倾听后会意识到：即便这单子要输给HubSpot，我最近收到四个SAP请求。我要赌一把。即使错了，也要赌一把。你得给他们这种权力……每周都要讨论："Jane，预算给你了。故事点给你了，你的10%给你了。这是我们现在为你建的，这是我们未来两季度计划的。你想调整未来两季度吗？因为我们还没写代码呢，如果你
想改变正在进行的项目？那你可以试试。但如果不这样做，可能会引发极大的混乱。不过为了销售业绩，你至少得装出客观的样子。（01:16:29）如果你对此过于情绪化，就会破坏整个团队的运作。你得说：“听着，我知道我们已经完成了80%的整合工作。但如果你非要我们搁置手头的一切，专注于一笔百万美元的交易——我们毕竟是初创公司，愿意为此全力以赴。但请问，这真的是你想要的吗？”如果每周都让他们以利益相关者的身份参与其中，奇迹就能发生。但我与之共事的产品副总裁们却很少这么做。我知道自己并非所有员工会议的参与者，但就我参加的会议和董事会会议而言，我从未见过这种意见交换的场景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This might be the same exact answer you just gave, but say you're a PM and a salesperson comes to you, "Hey, we're about to close this deal. We just need this one feature. Can we just get this on the roadmap?," what's the best way to help that sales person understand why it's not happening, help them feel like, "Okay, I get it"? Is it exactly what just said? "Okay, we could change everything. Here's the story points you have this quarter."
turns.zh: 或许你刚刚给出的回答完全一样，但假设你是一位产品经理，销售人员来找你说：“嘿，我们马上就要签下这笔订单了。只需要这一个功能，能不能把它加到路线图里？”怎样才能让销售人员明白为什么这件事无法实现，并让他们觉得“好吧，我理解了”？是刚刚说的那个办法吗？“好吧，我们可以改变一切。这是你们本季度已有的故事点。”

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Well, are you assuming that PM is the head of product or empowered enough to make the decisions?
turns.zh: 那么，你是假设产品经理是产品负责人吗？还是有足够权力做决策？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd say, yeah, that PM could put something on the roadmap if they think it's important.
turns.zh: 我觉得是的，如果产品经理认为某个功能很重要，他们是可以把它加到路线图里的。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: The reason I'm a little confused, just because I want to get it right, is what I'm hearing, which maybe isn't what you said. What I'm hearing is, a junior IC rep is talking to a more mid-level product person about the roadmap, and you want to have that. That's one of the reasons we actually go to the office. Because those discussions don't happen on Zoom, Lenny. They don't happen. And you want those discussions to happen, but you don't actually want them empowered. You want them to say, "Listen, I will talk to my boss." That's the right answer. It's too confusing. (01:17:58): This stress between product and sales is a good thing. It's a sign of a well-run B2B company when there is stress between product and sales. It's a good sign. If there's no stress, you're not in enough deals. You're not in enough deals if there's no stress. But the stress has to have enough process, even in a startup, that it doesn't break because your question alludes to the fact it can break organizations again and again. People get people resented on either side. (01:18:27): This is one thing where the answer has to be, "Look, we can chat about it over lunch. We can chat about this, and actually, you've got a good idea. You're an individual contributor. I'm going to tell my boss, on Monday, that I think we should do that. I'm going to use a little social capital and say we should do this," but you got to push the decisions up. That's as far as you're going to make recommendations. Otherwise, instead of that one stressful conversation with the VP, you've got a hundred, you've got 10 times a hundred, and again, they're fun lunch conversations, but they'll wreck you.
turns.zh: 我有点困惑的原因是，我想准确理解你的意思，但我听到的可能和你说的不同。我听到的是初级IC代表在和中级产品人员讨论路线图，而你希望这样的对话发生。这就是我们去办公室的原因。这种讨论不会在Zoom上进行，Lenny。真的不会。如果你希望这种讨论发生，但又不想赋予他们权力，那就让他们说：“听着，我会去和我的老板沟通。”这才是正确的做法。这太令人困惑了。（01:17:58）：产品和销售之间的这种压力是件好事。如果产品和销售之间存在压力，这说明一家B2B公司运作良好。没有压力是件好事，但前提是没有太多交易。如果没有压力，那说明交易量不足。但即使在初创公司，这种压力也必须有足够的流程来约束，否则会失控，因为你的问题暗示这种情况可能会让组织一次又一次地崩溃。双方的人会互相怨恨。（01:18:27）：在这种情况下，答案应该是：“听着，我们可以在午餐时聊聊这个。我们可以讨论这个想法，实际上你有个好主意。你是个人贡献者。我周一会告诉我的老板，我觉得我们应该这么做。我会动用一些社交资本，建议我们这么做。”但你必须把决策权上移。你的职责仅限于提出建议。否则，你就不是和VP进行一次紧张对话，而是要面对一百次甚至一百倍的对话。这些午餐时的轻松交谈固然有趣，但最终会把你累垮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the advice there is, basically, "Talk to your manager, I'll talk to my manager. They need to hash this out. It's not my call."
turns.zh: 所以基本建议就是：“和你的经理谈谈，我也会和我的经理谈谈。他们需要把这事解决。这不是我的决定。”

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: I think you got to push it up and I think you got to force the VP of Sales and the VP of Product to have this weekly meeting about the budget, and that will force them to have enough, just enough organization on their team so that it can all be surfaced up. Because that means they each have to have a meeting with their team for 30 minutes each week and say, "I'm going to put up on the whiteboard guys, so my sales team's going to say ... And I've been to many of these meetings where you force the sales team to force rank what they want and you end up, I tell you, Lenny, 100% of the time in the sales meeting, when you do a whiteboard force rank, you end up walking out with very different outputs than when you start the meeting in sales 100% of the time. (01:19:36): On the product side, you need to do the converse. You just need to say, "We owe sales 10% of our points, so in our team meeting, we're going to put in 15 minutes of our team meeting and we're going to make sure we have the priorities right from the sales team. Let's go over what I got from Linda. This is what she says. Is she wrong? Should we do something? How can we help the sales team be even more successful? And what inputs is the team hearing?" And they can raise their hand and say, "Look, I just had this all the way conversation with Bobby, but honestly, Lenny, I can build a HubSpot integration in a day." "What? I thought it was really hard." "No, I did it my last company. And listen, actually, we can actually outsource it to Bob and Linda at this agency I know for 20 grand. They'll build it next week." That's a magical moment. That's a magical moment. But you've got to each have these parallel meetings. The good thing, that tension can become debilitating. We've all seen those fights, those almost fights that break out, and they come from a place of passion, but you got to have structure.
turns.zh: 我觉得你得推动这个进程，让销售副总裁和产品副总裁每周开一次预算会议。这能迫使他们在团队层面加强组织协调，从而把问题暴露出来。毕竟他们每周都要和团队开30分钟的会议，说：“我要把这些写在白板上，然后让销售团队……”我参加过很多这样的会议，当你强制销售团队对需求进行排序时，每次结束时得到的结果都和会议开始时大相径庭。（01:19:36）：在产品端，策略则相反。你只需要说：“我们欠销售团队10%的业绩指标，所以在团队会议上，我们要用15分钟时间，确保优先事项与销售团队一致。让我们看看我从琳达那里收集的信息。她提了哪些建议？我们是否需要调整？如何能帮助销售团队取得更大成功？团队又有哪些需求？” 团队成员可以举手发言：“看，我刚和鲍比讨论过这个问题。但说实话，伦尼，我一天就能开发出HubSpot集成功能。”“什么？我以为这很难呢？” “不，我在上家公司就做过。听着，我们可以把这项工作外包给认识的某家代理公司，只需2万美元，他们下周就能完成。” 这就是神奇的时刻。但双方必须同时召开这样的会议。这种紧张关系可能会演变成破坏性冲突。我们都见过那种爆发的激烈争执，虽源于热情，但必须要有规矩约束。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great advice. Another trend I've been noticing is that product teams are taking on P&L responsibilities and revenue goals. What's your sense of, is that good? Is that bad? How do you think about that for product teams?
turns.zh: 很棒的建议。我注意到另一个趋势是，产品团队正逐渐承担损益责任和收入目标。您怎么看？这对产品团队是好事还是坏事？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: You want everyone to be aligned on the big picture revenue goal for the end of the year. Is the question, you mean having financial bonuses and stuff tied to hitting the plan?
turns.zh: 您的意思是让所有人围绕年底的总体收入目标达成一致？问题在于，是否会将财务奖金等与达成计划挂钩？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: More that their KPIs and their OKRs are essentially this much revenue, you need to drive this much revenue from your experiments, from your product launches.
turns.zh: 更重要的是，他们的KPI和OKR本质上就是要实现这么多收入目标，必须通过实验和产品发布来达成这些目标。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: As you can see, I have a lot of opinions on things here that are data-driven and they're live experience. This one, I need another year in the oven, and I'll tell you why. I'll tell you why. What happened in the last 18 months is, in customer success, which is, in the old days, it was related to product. Now, it's less so, which I think is unfortunate. In customer success, in the last 18 months, this happened all across the industry. 24 months ago, customer success's goal was happy customers, measured in retention, sometimes NRR, net retention with upsells, sometimes with GRR, just logos, how many logos. That was your only job, happy customers. Happy customers. (01:21:35): Then, things got harder in many areas of B2B, and every customer success team last year, their goal was revenue. You need to bring in more revenue from existing base, and it destroyed customer relationships. There is a leading public company, I will not name them, I'm a positive guy. I will tell you, a company we all have used for years and loved, and they did this to their customer success team. And they came to us last year, we paid $299 a month for this product for our team. They asked us for $50,000 upfront or said they would turn it off that day. That week. Maybe it was that week. $50,000. That's what happens when you weaponize ... (01:22:10): So customer success, and I know this is going to trigger some people, but it is true, when I talk to leaders, customer success got weaponized and I don't like it, okay? I don't like it as a product. All founders are product people, I think. I don't like it as a product because I think it's bad for customers. That experience I got was horrific, wasn't it? That $50,000, being told. And it got walked back. And the fact that it got walked back is almost even worse because it wasn't true. It was a threat. So do I want to weaponize the product team? I want the product team aligned with revenue. These are the tough decisions for founders. But I think we're going to regret, to some extent, weaponizing teams that we don't need to weaponize. (01:22:50): Having said that, I will tell you, and again, no knock on Adobe, but when I was a VP at Adobe, and it was a long time ago, when product was in another building, in some cases, that was not great. And I love Scott and the whole team, it was a great experience, but I can just tell you, what I learned is, that did not work for me as an agile guy, having groups that would do this work in isolation. (01:23:08): And the problem was they would never talk to a customer. So I know I want product constantly talking to the customer. I know I want the VP of product with a lot of equity, wanting to hit the bookings number for the year. Do I want your average PM weaponized and forced to bring in revenue from an experimental feature when everyone agreed it's the test we're going to run? We only can run so many. You say, should they have revenue for new feature launches, for new product expansions, for new things? Yes, but everyone's got to make that decision. There aren't that many of us that have 1,000 extra engineers sitting around with nothing to do. (01:23:44): Even the smallest experiment, no matter what it says on the internet, again, that we release 100 a day, I would argue bringing any product extension to market's very expensive and risky because you're taking away from something else. These are expensive decisions, and if you punish people for the mistakes in product, this is something that big companies are actually better at than startups, which is, they don't fire you if the new initiative fails. Because then, no one at a big company would ever join the new initiative. There are exceptions, but no one at Adobe or Google would work on the new product if you got fired if it didn't hit $100 million its first year. (01:24:21): One thing I saw that was very, and I don't know how to bring to startups in my big company experience, was it's liberating to some extent to let people fail, up to a point. It's liberating. Because the cost of failure in a startup is so high. It's just so high. I know that's not what the exact question, and ask me in a year, but my advice is, just be careful that you don't weaponize functions.
turns.zh:
正如你所见，我对这里许多基于数据的观点和实际经验都很有见解。但这个观点还需要再锤炼一年，我来解释一下原因。过去18个月里，客户成功部门的定位发生了转变——在传统观念中，客户成功通常与产品紧密相连，但如今这种关联性正在减弱，我认为这很遗憾。过去18个月里，整个行业的客户成功团队都面临着挑战。24个月前，客户成功部门的核心目标是提升客户满意度，衡量指标包括客户留存率、净推荐值（NRR），甚至是净复购率（GRR）和品牌知名度（logos）。那时你的唯一任务就是让客户满意，仅此而已。（01:21:35）但去年许多B2B领域的客户成功团队开始把目标转向收入增长——他们要求从现有客户群中挖掘更多收入，这最终损害了客户关系。有一家大型上市公司（我不会点名，我是个乐观派），我们多年来一直喜爱并使用他们的产品。去年他们突然威胁要关闭客户成功团队，除非我们提前支付5万美元，否则就立即停用服务。这笔交易最终被撤回，但这种威胁手段本身就令人不齿。（01:22:10）所以客户成功部门被武器化了，这让我很不舒服。作为产品出身的创始人，我认为这对客户关系有害。那种被勒索的经历太可怕了。（01:23:08）话说回来，Adobe的情况也不容乐观。我在Adobe担任VP时，产品团队与其他部门分开办公，这其实不太理想。虽然我很欣赏Scott和整个团队，但我必须承认，产品团队被武器化是错误的做法。（01:23:44）即便是最微小的实验项目，别管网上吹嘘的每日100个实验，任何新功能的上线都极其昂贵且高风险，因为这必然会挤占其他资源。这些都是高风险决策，如果因为产品团队的失误就惩罚员工，大公司在这方面比初创公司做得更好。毕竟大公司即便新产品失败也不会轻易裁员。
创新举措往往会失败。因为在大公司里，没人会愿意加入新项目。当然也有例外，但在 Adobe 或谷歌这样的公司，如果新产品首年营收达不到 1 亿美元，你就会被解雇。在这种情况下，没人会愿意为新项目付出努力。（01:24:21）：我注意到一个在大公司工作时很难向初创企业传递的理念——在一定程度上，允许员工失败其实是一种解脱。这很自由，因为初创企业的失败成本实在太高了。太高了。我知道这不是问题的核心，但若干年后再问我，我给出的建议是：务必注意别将职能部门变成用来打击异己的工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I probably should have clarified. I think this is mostly true in PLG companies where most of the growth is coming from product, but I imagine the advice is still the same, as be careful putting too much pressure on the product team to focus on revenue.
turns.zh: 或许我该解释得更清楚些。我认为这在PLG（产品生命周期管理）公司中尤为明显，因为它们的增长主要来自产品本身，但我相信核心建议依然适用：切忌给产品团队施加过大压力，迫使他们过度关注营收。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Well, that's how you get dark stuff. Back in the day, I remember my sister worked at Vistaprint for online business cards, and her entire job was to force people to buy upsell of additional products on the checkout page they didn't want to buy. That was her whole job. And she was paid a large variable comp to get people to buy third party products without realizing in their checkout, and it worked. That's all she did for three years was figure out dark stuff, I mean, darkish, grayish stuff so that when I bought my business card, I also bought GoDaddy and 11 other things that I didn't want. It works, but it doesn't create high NPS, does it?

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: The number one thing they can do, and this is very tactical, at the end of each meeting, because again, both of them are good middlers, the head of product and the founders are good demos, they're good at talking shop, they're good at talking in the industry, they're good at talking workflows. 托马斯·曾加里斯（Tomas Tsangaris）专门做了一场关于免费试用和免费试用期的SaaStr演讲。内容很精彩，但有一点你可能不知道——作为一个业内老手，我深知一个历史事实：互联网上14天免费试用的政策，最初源于Salesforce销售团队在专注中小企业客户时想在当月完成交易的需求。因此，他们将免费试用期限从30天缩短至14天，但并没有证据表明这对客户更有利，也没有证据证明能提高用户活跃度。他们只是想在当月达成交易。

（01:31:41）：这些数据指标需要谨慎解读。特别是面对产品团队时，要确保他们以客户为中心。如今的Salesforce已转型为面向大企业的产品，但早期团队为了让销售人员快速达成交易，强制将免费试用期缩短至14天。Slack和Zoom直到最近才发现无限期免费试用效果不错，Canva也是如此。Slack、Canva和最近的Zoom都能耐心等待四年实现转化——这些都是伟大的公司。

（01:32:12）：这些决策只有创始人才能做出。多年前我写过一篇文章，问“谁是你的‘免费副总裁’？”因为谁会专门设立这个职位？你认识有‘免费副总裁’的公司吗？我见过‘增长副总裁’、‘产品副总裁’，但面对庞大的免费用户群，谁来负责‘免费业务’？几乎没有公司有专门的‘免费副总裁’。通常这是产品团队和CEO的合作职位，但即便如此也需要专人负责，而我们至今没有这样的职位。

（01:32:49）：在试用期越来越严格的当下，要警惕那些短期建议。例如，VC们常提的‘改用年付制’就是糟糕建议。这种建议来自从未打造过产品、脱离实际的人。在Excel表格里看似美观，但实际效果如何？

好的，用户让我把一段英文翻译成中文。首先，我需要仔细阅读原文，理解每个句子的意思。这段文字主要讲的是销售中的数据分析、价格上涨、客户保留等问题，涉及到商业策略和产品管理。翻译时要注意专业术语的准确性，比如“PLG motion”可能需要保留英文缩写，或者找到合适的中文对应词。

接下来，处理一些口语化的表达，比如“bounce”在这里指的是用户流失率，可能需要翻译成“流失率”或“用户流失”。还有“win-loss meetings”是销售团队常用的术语，应该译为“胜负分析会议”或类似表达。

然后，注意保持原文的语气和风格。例如，发言者对价格上涨的批评，要传达出严厉的质问语气，比如“Did you earn it?”需要翻译得口语化且带有质问的意味。

另外，涉及到具体数据和年份的部分，比如“2023年”，要确保翻译准确，避免歧义。还有“ARR”这样的术语，可能需要保留英文缩写并加注释，或者直接翻译为“年度经常性收入”。

最后，检查整体译文的流畅性和专业性，确保术语一致，语句通顺，没有语法错误。同时，注意文化差异，比如“free editions”翻译成“免费版本”即可，不需要额外解释。

总之，翻译过程中要兼顾准确性和自然流畅，确保专业术语正确，同时保持原文的语气和意图，让中文读者能清晰理解内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Almost 600,000.
turns.zh: 差不多60万。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Okay. 600,000. Now, not all of them convert, do they?
turns.zh: 好的。60万。不过，并非所有用户都会完成转化，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, no. That's exactly how I look at it. It's kind of this Brian Belfort is this... Yeah.
turns.zh: 别，别。我的看法就是这样。布莱恩·贝尔福特这种人……对吧。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: What about the 590,000 of them that love Lenny that don't convert, right?
turns.zh: 那剩下59万个喜欢莱尼却不转化的人呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: If you over monetize them, then Lenny's community doesn't exist if you over monetize them. But when you bring in a VP of sales for Lenny and a VP of growth and... You can't expect them to care as much about that long tail as you, right?
turns.zh: 如果你过度商业化他们，莱尼的社区就没了。但如果你给莱尼招个销售副总裁和增长副总裁……你总不能指望他们像你一样重视那些长尾用户吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love your passion around this. So, what I'm hearing partly is you're a big fan of freemium, essentially, right? And the benefits of product-led growth where there's something you could just use indefinitely, or do you still think that's a trial where it needs to end at some point? Or is it just like, "No, freemium is great in a lot of cases."
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你对此的热情。那么，我听到的部分内容是，你实际上是免费增值模式（freemium）的忠实拥趸，对吧？而产品主导型增长（product-led growth）的优势在于，用户可以无限期地使用某项服务，或者你仍然认为这只是一个需要在某个时间点结束的试用期？或者你只是觉得，"不，免费增值模式在很多情况下都很棒。"

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Listen, I'm a big fan of long tails when they work. They don't always work for enterprise products. I'm a big fan of delivering more value than you take out for your customers. And I am a big fan overall of free, because, and I know you'll agree with me this, every founder figures this out at some point, free products are better software. Products that cannot offer a free edition cut corners because they don't have to be good at onboarding. The products that do not have a free edition have human beings that bridge the gap between buying and deployment. And that's okay at ServiceNow, and that's okay in certain products, but the best products invest the engineering cycles to have a free edition. Whether that's truly free, whether it's an extended free trial, whether it's a long tail or a medium tail, the amount of... All of your product is better if people can actually, if you have a free edition, all your customers benefit, even your enterprise customers benefit, they all benefit.
turns.zh: 听着，当长尾策略奏效时，我绝对是它的忠实拥趸。但它并不总是适用于企业级产品。我坚信为客户创造超出其贡献价值的产品至关重要。总的来说，我支持免费模式，因为——我知道你会认同这一点，每个创始人都会在某个阶段意识到这一点——免费产品往往是更优质的软件。那些无法提供免费版本的产品往往在用户获取环节偷工减料。而那些有免费版本的产品，则需要人力来衔接购买与部署之间的空白环节。在ServiceNow这样的公司，以及某些产品中，这没什么问题，但最优秀的产品会投入工程资源来打造免费版本。无论是真正的免费、延长免费试用、长尾或中尾策略，只要能让用户受益——尤其是企业客户——整个产品体系都会获益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This idea of VP of free, I think technically it's probably the head of growth for a PLG company or the person leading the self-serve part of the business.
turns.zh: VP of Free这个职位，我认为从技术层面看，它可能是PLG公司增长部门的负责人或自助服务业务的负责人。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: But even in the organizations I work with that have those structures, that person is focused on monetizing that tail. Who stands up for the 590,000 other readers of Lenny? Who's their champion?
turns.zh: 但即使在我合作过的那些有这种架构的公司里，那个人也专注于将长尾用户变现。谁会为Lenny的59万其他读者发声？谁是他们的捍卫者？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and you're 100% right. That's exactly how I think about the newsletter. There's this free audience and ideas over time, they get convinced, "This is worth my money and let's give it a shot."
turns.zh: 是啊，你完全正确。这正是我对新闻通讯的看法。有一个免费的受众群体，随着时间推移，用户会被说服："这东西值我的钱，让我们试试看。"

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, yeah.
turns.zh: 所以，是啊。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: And your growth person, let's say 1% converts. I'm just making that up. Going from 1 to 1.1 actually is a big deal at that scale or 1.2, right? That's okay. But you've got to nurture the 490,000, not spend all the calories just ramming the paid edition through, right? But only it's a fun thing, because once you hit a little bit of scale, this is part of your job as founders and product leaders is who's going to be this VP of free? It's not growth. I don't think it's the growth team or something. They got to hit their goal when their goal is to get another half million out of the newsletter this year. And that's their bonuses side to it. You think they're going to work on the free ones? No chance.
turns.zh: 而你的增长团队，比如说，1%转化率。我随便举个例子。从1%提升到1.1%，对于这样的规模来说确实意义重大，对吧？没错。但你必须培育那49万用户，而不是把所有精力都投入到强推付费版本上，对吧？但这其实挺有趣的，因为一旦达到一定规模，创始人和产品负责人的职责之一就是：谁来担任VP of Free？这不是增长团队的任务。我不认为是增长团队或相关部门的责任。当他们的目标是今年从新闻通讯中再挖掘50万用户时，他们必须达成目标。这是他们奖金体系的一部分。你觉得他们会去研究免费用户吗？没门儿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense. Oh man, there's so many things I can go into and want to go into. I also want to let you go. So with that, is there anything else, Jason, that you wanted to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round? Anything you want to leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 有道理。天哪，有太多我想深入探讨的内容了。但既然如此，杰森，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？有什么想留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: I think just make this the year of the customer guys. And I really think that sales has been under so much pressure the last 18 months. Customer success has changed. Product teams have to step up. This is your time to do great things this year as product people. Be the voice of the customer. Be the VP of free, be the whatever. Be the champion. Stick your neck out. Work harder, folks. Work harder. The funnest part of anything in startups is working hard, but in product it's extra fun. By working harder, you have the more fun conversations. Find the delight in... The delight in product is making customers happy. It's not worth it otherwise. Otherwise, it's drudgery and it's endless PRDs and Gantt charts and mindless discussions. Make your customers happier this year, you will be happy. This is the year of product and we all get a pass for whatever bad deeds we did or mediocre deeds we did in 2023, get back and be the vanguard in your companies. (01:40:53): Startups need, and bigger companies, they need someone to inject energy again, in many cases. Energy has been lost. And it would be great if product can do it and say, "Listen, let's do something, even if we're not exactly sure how to get more leads, okay? Even if we're not exactly sure what to do, there's one thing under our control is the code we write and the product we ship. Let's do three great things this year. Let's just do them not good, great. Let's do three great." And what you'll find is the whole company will respond, including sales, including marketing, including... If we start shipping great thing. Few things inspire teams more than when you're shipping great products. So, be... If you weren't the leaders the last two years, if you were being forced to weaponize your customer base somehow ship three great things this year. That's my challenge. Ship three great things.
turns.zh:
我觉得今年应该把客户放在首位伙计们。我真的认为过去18个月里，销售部门承受了巨大的压力。客户成功部门的职责已经发生了变化。产品团队必须挺身而出。今年作为产品从业者，你们有机会大显身手了。要成为客户的代言人，要扮演免费增值产品的VP，要做任何你想做的“冠军”。勇于突破，努力工作，伙计们。努力工作。创业公司最有趣的部分就是努力工作，而在产品领域，这份乐趣更是加倍。通过更加努力的工作，你们能参与更有趣的讨论。在产品中找到乐趣，就是让客户满意。否则这一切都毫无意义。否则就只是枯燥的PRD文档、甘特图和无意义的讨论。今年让客户更开心，你们自己也会开心。这是产品之年，我们都能被原谅过去在2023年犯过的错误或做过的平庸之举，重新在公司里成为先锋。

（01:40:53）：创业公司需要，规模更大的公司也需要有人能再次注入活力。在很多情况下，活力已经流失了。如果产品团队能做到这一点，那就太棒了。比如说：“听着，让我们做点什么吧，就算我们不确定如何获取更多线索，就算我们不确定该做什么，但至少我们能掌控代码和产品发布。今年我们要做三件了不起的事。别做得一般，要做得出色。要做三件了不起的事。”你会发现整个公司都会响应，包括销售团队、市场团队……只要我们开始交付出色的产品，团队的积极性就会被激发。所以，要么……如果你过去两年不是领导者，如果你被迫以某种方式利用客户资源，那今年就交付三件了不起的事吧。这就是我的挑战。交付三件了不起的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. This is the year of product, that might be the title of this podcast.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。这是产品之年，这或许可以作为这个播客的标题。

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Jason, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 杰森，我们迎来激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Okay. I'm worried about the first one, but go for it.
turns.zh: 好的。第一个问题让我有点担心，但还是来吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're very non-surprising, because they're always the same. What are two or three books you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 这些问题一点也不意外，因为它们总是老生常谈。你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: That's the one I just want to take a pass on. I know they're the same. I read more than anybody else in the planet, but I wish I had those two great, great books that have changed my mind in the last 12 months, but hopefully I've added some value. But this one, I think I got to take a mulligan on it [inaudible 01:42:14] perfect answer.
turns.zh: 这个我就不想回答了。我知道它们都一样。我是这个星球上阅读量最大的人，但我希望能找到两本在过去12个月里真正改变了我的思维的优秀书籍，但希望我能带来一些价值。但这个问题，我觉得我得先考虑一下[01:42:14]完美回答。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Acceptable answer. Is there a favorite movie or TV show that you really enjoy?
turns.zh: 可以接受的回答。你有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Oh, the Terminal List.
turns.zh: 哦，《终极杀手》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The Terminal List?
turns.zh: 《终极杀手》？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: The Terminal List, yeah. I'm not into the Chris Pratt. I'm not into that goofy superhero movies he does, and I know people like it, but The Terminal List, it's pretty, it's I got it, it's written by this ex Navy SEAL that I think tech people don't read the... Everyone, but outside of tech reads this author, but Amazon did this thing with The Terminal List and I think the reason it gripped me, it's like this post, it's like a lot of tech is right now is we're trying to do the right things, but are we doing the right things? It's just confusing. So this one, I couldn't put down, The Terminal List. That was my favorite show. The other one, the one I liked that I couldn't believe. You want the second one? Even though as product people, Maverick, and I'll tell you why. This movie Maverick, okay, you wouldn't think I'd be a Maverick guy, but the quality of this product, it was so high. (01:43:18): And what's interesting, you remember Maverick was supposed to come out before COVID, right? And Tom Cruise said no. He's like, "This is such a good product, we're going to wait years for this thing to come out." I'm like, " I'm not going to like this. I mean, cocktail was pretty good, but I'm not going to..." But as a product, when... I've watched this movie three times from a product perspective and just like software, when something is done that well, no wasted calories, no... You see everything tied together. That's the kind of software we love, right? It just delights us when it works better than we expected. So, those are my two.
turns.zh: 是啊，我对《终极杀戮》没什么兴趣。我对克里斯·普拉特的那些超级英雄电影也不感冒，虽然我知道很多人喜欢，但《终极杀戮》拍得挺不错的。我知道它是前海军海豹突击队成员写的，我觉得科技圈的人可能不太读他的作品，不过这部作品确实火了，对吧？亚马逊对它的推广很到位，而我之所以被它吸引，可能是因为它和我们现在面临的困境很相似——我们总想做正确的事，但又不确定自己是否真做对了。所以这部剧我一口气看完了，它是我的最爱。另一部我喜欢的作品，简直难以置信。想听第二部吗？虽然作为产品经理，我对《壮志凌云：马弗里克》没啥好感，但这部作品的质量确实高超。（01:43:18）有意思的是，你记得《壮志凌云》本该在新冠疫情前上映的，对吧？但汤姆·克鲁斯拒绝了。他说：“这部作品太棒了，我们宁愿等几年也不愿仓促上映。”我当时想：“我肯定不爱看这种片子，不过《鸡尾酒》倒是不错。”但从产品角度来看，这部电影堪称典范——没有任何冗余，所有情节环环相扣。这正是我们喜爱的软件品质，对吧？当它比预期更出色时，那种愉悦感简直难以言表。接下来是我的两个心头好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also did all his own stunts, which I think is a good metaphor for the VP of product, maybe being involved in sales?
turns.zh: 你还亲自完成了所有特技动作，我觉得这对产品副总裁来说是个绝佳的比喻，或许也适用于参与销售工作的副总裁？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: Actually do the work.
turns.zh: 亲力亲为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Oh man, I'm stretching it. Okay, next question. You answered a few of these already, but do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask when you're interviewing salespeople, especially?
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。天啊，我扯远了。下一个问题。你已经回答过一些问题，但有没有特别喜欢问销售人员的面试题？特别是初级销售？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: I answered it, but I'll bring it up again in case you do it again, is, "What do you want to do your first 14 days to head of product or head of sales? What do you want to do your first 14 days?" It's not a technical 30-day plan, you don't have to do 28 slides. It's what I call a Colombo question. Not that I really watch Colombo, but Colombo is this old detective on TV who, I don't know if you ever, he would ask these dumb questions, right? And then the murderer would thought Colombo was so dumb, but by the end of the episode he'd always incriminate himself because the question. So, when I interview, I always do Colombo questions. They're never tough ones, right? They're always nice. I don't know if I'm nice, I'm honest, but the interview [inaudible 01:44:42]. But Lenny, what would you do your first 14 days as VP of product here? And they don't want to visit customers. Don't hire them for either all sales or product. Just don't hire them.
turns.zh: 我回答过，但再提一次以防你再问：你上任产品或销售副总裁后的头14天想做什么？这不是技术类的30天计划书，不需要28张幻灯片。我称之为“科伦坡式提问”。不是说我真的看过《科伦坡》，但那部老电视剧里的警探，总爱问些看似愚蠢的问题，结果凶手总在结尾自露马脚。所以我面试时总用这种科伦坡式提问。绝不是刁难，而是友好提问。我不知道自己算不算友好，至少很诚实。（面试时[01:44:42]）但莱尼，你上任产品副总裁后头14天想做什么？他们不想拜访客户。别雇佣既做销售又做产品的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've got the answer now. That's exactly what I was going to say. Next question, what is a favorite product that you have recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 我现在知道答案了。这正是我想说的。下一个问题，最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Lemkin
turns.en: My two aren't really amazing, but I'll answer them. I love this Opus Clip app for making clips from video. I know you have a whole team, so you probably don't need it, but I produce a lot. I mean, a lot of us do content marketing, right? Whoever does it. I produce a lot of content. I don't have enough time to do this. So, the only AI tool that I've found helpful so far is Opus Clip, which takes all of the incredible amount of YouTube content we have, force ranks it and turns it into 59 second clips. And I'm a case study on the website, I tried the earlier products. They were almost there, right? But it's not, is it as good as a clip team? Right? Is it? No. (01:45:41): But literally in 60 seconds, what's interesting is it can do something, I don't have time to, I could never make YouTube clips. I could never make Instagram shorts. I could never make... It just would never happen, right? It would never happen. And the fact that one product enables you to do something at a minimum viable quality you couldn't do before, I'm a super fan. It's pretty interesting. So, that's my favorite. And my other one is this one. This is the folding phone that's finally as good as a normal phone. See, there's The Terminal List that I've got folded up and it just works.

turns.zh: 任何企业，无论多么奇特，只要规模够大，做到行业顶尖，总是值得研究的。拿案例研究来说，比如最佳咖啡师、最佳某某领域的专家——这些本身可能并不引人注目，但背后总有精彩的故事。SaaStr 也是一个社区，就像你们现在经营的社区一样。我们在 2011 年、2012 年初为 B2B 创业者创立这个社区时，人们还觉得这很疯狂。如今看来已不足为奇。我们积累了大量内容，开始举办活动和聚会。我自己从未参加过太多聚会，但 2012 和 2013 年我亲自参与组织时，竟然有 1000 人参与。（01:50:56）：如今大家可能觉得这很正常，但十年前对于 B2B 领域而言，这确实令人惊讶。当时人们会问：“为什么这么多人聚集在这里？我们以为只有六个人对 B2B 感兴趣。”后来我们举办大型活动，2015 年一天的 SaaStr 年会吸引了 3000 人（含晚宴），之后规模不断扩大。如今我们每年能聚集约 1 万至 1.2 万人。这些变化意味着什么？它不再是新鲜事物。我不再是唯一制作 B2B 内容的人，也不再是唯一出售公司的人。如今有更多成功的创业者，他们比我优秀得多。我自己很少做播客，因为我远不如你们专业。例如，我每季度才做一次节目。（01:51:34）：但这些活动已成为规模化创业者的聚会平台，他们的公司规模在 100 万到 2000 万美元之间。尤其是非硅谷的创业者，比如海斯谷之外的创业者，他们缺乏本地社区支持。最初让我惊讶的是，有那么多国际参与者不远万里飞来湾区。我记得有位来自澳大利亚珀斯的创业者参加了首日下午的活动。我说：“感谢你的到来，但这太麻烦了。”他回答：“我来不是为了你，而是因为珀斯没有像我这样的人。”所以这个社区逐渐形成了自己的生态。其中有很多经验教训。我本无意举办大规模活动，只是想举办聚会，因为我也有像你们这样的社区。一切都是偶然。关键在于，活动成本极高，而且存在奇特的增长曲线。我认为所有创业者、初创公司都应该为自己的客户举办活动——至少我写过关于牛排晚宴的文章。只要把客户和潜在客户聚集在一起，就能促进销售。活动不必花费数百万美元，也不必过于奢华。可以是 Roots Chrises 这样的活动，或者任何形式。关键是让他们聚在一起。

花1000万美元才能让灯光亮起。现在，我所说的"让灯光亮起"可能有点夸张，但这确实就是成本。想在湾区或拉斯维加斯举办一场大规模活动，每位参会者大约需要花费1000美元。不是小型活动，也不是为期一天的会议，而是多天的盛会，对吧？视听设备费用150万美元，餐饮费用150万美元，帐篷搭建费用80万美元。我可以继续列举下去。一旦活动收入达到2000万、3000万美元，悄然间就会有上市公司介入。（01:55:04）：他们有像Margins这样的软件，但在此之前，成本实在太高了，对吧？我刚开始做这些活动时，采访了2020年3月之前负责活动的技术公司高管。他们几乎都放弃了这项业务，这是一个有趣的旁支话题。像Twilio、Marketo这样的巨头，他们都会问："活动办得怎么样了？"得到的回答都是一样的。"嗯，我们赚了150万美元。" "哦，亏了200万美元。"每个人都亏了200万美元。每个公司都亏了200万美元。你可以从财务报表中看到，就连Zoom这样的大公司在Zoomtopia上也宣布亏损了多少钱。所以这是一项糟糕的业务。我想说的是它存在规模不经济。Lenny的小型免费聚会成本为零，对吧？在Cloudflare办公室举办的活动也是零成本。（01:55:50）：而在希尔顿B酒店举办的活动可能每人200美元，但大规模活动每人要1000美元，对吧？即使像旧金山的Moscone这样的大型场地，费用可能更高。你要预订15到20万间酒店客房才能在Moscone举办活动，对吧？所以我不知道...我们可以把这当作Lenny的副播客，供感兴趣的人听。但规模不经济的现象确实存在。有几家上市公司，比如Lions、Money 2020、Shoptalk，规模达到了SaaStr级别。他们拼凑起这些极具盈利能力的上市公司。但所有这些公司至少要达到2000万到3000万美元的收入门槛，因为你必须突破1000万美元的净利润门槛。对吧？（01:56:33）：这意味着我们每年要花14到16个月的时间筹备SaaStr年会，因为如果超支600万或800万美元，那可就没那么好玩了。2020年3月，我们是首批因新冠疫情被取消的重大活动。RSA安全大会在那之前一周因为疫情取消了。所以我们一天就损失了1000万美元，花了很长时间才摆脱这个困境，Lenny，尤其是我们不赚钱，所以时间更长，但这些努力都是值得的。（01:57:04）：我知道你不做传统活动，但你在社区里举办聚会，我知道这些很值得。我知道这些很值得。把客户聚集在一起，把社区团结起来，我们之前线下就讨论过这个问题。二线、三线活动我认为不值得，因为它们吸引不到最优秀的人才。这是事实。大多数人，结果发现我们的创始人是我们的核心ICP。他们平均每年参加两次活动，两次活动，对吧？然后他们会参加其他牛排晚宴。所以如果你参加他们参加的两次活动中的一个，你可能会碰到Jeff Lawson或Eric Juan之类的人。他们可能会参加其中一次，但他们不会参加三线到十线的活动。他们不会参加这些活动。
